title: Effects of acoustic environment on work in private office rooms and open-plan offices – longitudinal study during relocation
research_question: To determine how the perceived work environment, especially acoustic environment, and its effects differed in private office rooms and in open-plan offices, using a longitudinal study during relocation.

participants.description: 31 professional workers (70% male, mean age 35, range 26-56) from a Finnish engineering services and maintenance company, who moved from private office rooms to open-plan offices. Their work tasks mainly required individual efforts.
participants.recruitment: Company suggested a questionnaire study; subjects were informed of two measurements and matched by mother's maiden name.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Old office building: Two-storey cellular office with thin building frame and single corridor plan. Small office rooms (approx. 10 m²) occupied by one person. Drywall partitions from floor to ceiling. Doors usually open to corridor. (Before relocation)

New office building: Two-storey building with a combination of small office rooms (not studied for this group) and open-plan offices. Open-plan offices were narrow (8m wide, approx. 25m long). Workstations enclosed on two or three sides with screens (127 cm or 165 cm height). Ceiling covered by perforated plasterboard (sound absorption class C, NRC=0.50). Walls and floor were acoustically reflecting. (After relocation)

measures.construct: Overall disturbance by indoor environmental factors
Satisfaction with work environment as a whole
Satisfaction with acoustical conditions as a whole
Disturbance to work types by sounds
Use of coping strategies due to sounds
Self-estimated wasted working time due to sounds
Ability to carry on a discussion without raising voice

measures.instrument: Omni-directional loudspeaker (Brüel & Kjær 4296) and microphone, real-time analyser (Brüel & Kjær 2260A)

mechanisms: Higher speech intelligibility (STI) and lower background noise in open-plan offices lead to increased disturbance by irrelevant speech.
Lack of acoustic and visual privacy in open-plan offices contributes to reduced satisfaction and increased distraction.
Modern and efficient ventilation and cooling systems in the new building improved thermal and air quality perceptions.
Individual differences in noise sensitivity and trait anxiety influence the perception of noise and symptoms.
Workers employ coping strategies to compensate for environmental factors that decrease performance ability.
moderators: Job type/work demandingness (individual cognitive work vs. teamwork)
Gender (women more noise-sensitive and disturbed by noise in open-plan offices)
Office type (private vs. open-plan) for gender effects on disturbance and coping
implementation_implications: Private office rooms are recommended for workers performing mainly individual and cognitively demanding work and needing confidential conversations.
Small interactive teams should be located in shared rooms, not large open-plan offices.
Anonymous private rooms should be provided for open-plan office workers for concentration-demanding work, paired work, or private conversations.
Alternative workstation types in the same office building should be encouraged to facilitate selection based on current work task and improve control over the work environment.
Common rules for behaviour should be created in each department, encouraging low speech levels, private phone calls in anonymous rooms, and not leaving mobile phones ringing.
Workers should be involved in workplace design and relocation processes managed by professionals.
Proper acoustic design of open-plan offices (screen height, enclosure, absorption material, speech masking) is crucial for improving satisfaction and reducing disturbance.

limitations: The study was conducted in a company that had already made all decisions regarding acoustic environment for the new office, limiting experimental control.
Only 31 out of 85 initial respondents completed the post-relocation questionnaire, leading to a small sample size.
The third questionnaire (1 year after relocation) had only 12 respondents, so results were not presented.
The study focused on professional workers whose work tasks mainly required individual efforts, limiting generalizability to other job types.
The noise level meter does not indicate which sounds are relevant to the worker and which are not, making it difficult to associate SPL variability with subjective disturbance.
The study did not properly investigate ways of coping in different office environments, despite its expected strong connection with work performance.
The study did not include acoustical measurements along with questionnaires in many previous studies, making direct comparisons difficult.
The study lacked a detailed description of the open-plan office type in many previous studies, which plays a fundamental role in acoustic perception and privacy.
The study did not investigate the effect of individual factors (e.g., noise sensitivity, extroversion, trait anxiety, locus of control) on noise perception in offices sufficiently.
The study did not include a more detailed analysis of work tasks to better associate cognitive laboratory findings with field work tasks.
The private office rooms studied had poorer acoustic conditions (low sound insulation) than typically obtained, potentially reducing the acoustic difference between office types.
